narrative:
The model estimates there’s a 34% chance you won’t pass your final year, which is above the 10% threshold that requires extra support. This doesn’t mean failure is certain, but it does mean the school has a duty to step in early so you can finish strong.

The prediction was shaped most by your family background. Your father’s education level was the single biggest factor pushing the model toward concern. While half of students who pass have a parent with higher education, your father only completed primary school, which the model sees as a risk. On the other hand, you’ve never failed a class before, and that track record helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Your clear ambition to go to university also worked in your favor, showing motivation that the model values.

Other details mattered less, but still played a role. For example, your parents live apart, which is uncommon among students who pass, and you don’t receive family tutoring at home, even though most of your classmates do. Yet you study 2–5 hours a week, which is typical, and your family relationships are rated very good, which is rarer and reassuring.

The next step is straightforward: attend the remedial courses the school offers. They’re designed to give you extra time and attention in the subjects that need it most. Use this as a chance to build confidence, ask questions, and stay on track for university. The model flagged risks, but it also saw strengths—your past success and your goals. With focused effort, you can shift the odds in your favor.
